restaurants.whyGo: East Village's own Italian rather than a Westfield unit, doing pizza and pasta for the people who actually live in the athletes' village.

restaurants.name: Bamboo Mat
restaurants.address: 21-24 Victory Parade, East Village, London E20 1FS, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Nikkei cooking - the Japanese-Peruvian tradition - which is a genuinely unexpected thing to find in Stratford and the reason to skip the chains.

restaurants.name: Kateh
restaurants.whyGo: A Michelin Bib Gourmand Persian kitchen in a small townhouse off Warwick Avenue, hung with Persian art and run more like a home than a restaurant.

restaurants.name: The Waterway
restaurants.whyGo: One of the largest canal-side terraces in London, right on the water at Little Venice, and the first thing in the area to fill up on a warm weekend.

restaurants.name: The Summerhouse
restaurants.whyGo: A New England-looking clapboard room right at the water's edge, doing seafood and fish and chips with the canal a metre from the table.
restaurants.signature: Fish and chips by the water

restaurants.name: Beany Green Little Venice
restaurants.whyGo: Australian brunch on the towpath with a big canal-side terrace, and the easiest good breakfast within walking distance of Paddington station.
restaurants.signature: Smashed avocado and a flat white

restaurants.name: The Town of Ramsgate
restaurants.address: 62 Wapping High St, London E1W 2PN, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A pub on this spot since at least 1545, long and narrow, opening onto a small river terrace beside Wapping Old Stairs and Execution Dock.
restaurants.signature: A pint on the river terrace

restaurants.name: The Captain Kidd
restaurants.address: The Captain Kidd, 108 Wapping High St, London E1W 2NE, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A converted warehouse laid out like a ship's hull, named for the pirate hanged a few yards away, with the biggest river terrace in Wapping.
restaurants.signature: A pint on the Thames terrace

restaurants.name: Turner's Old Star
restaurants.whyGo: An 1830 back-street local that JMW Turner is said to have owned and run for a mistress - the last plain, unrenovated pub left in Wapping.
restaurants.signature: A quiet pint away from the river crowds

restaurants.name: Toulouse Lautrec
restaurants.style: French brasserie with a jazz club upstairs
restaurants.whyGo: Three floors of a converted pub run by three brothers since 2008: a rustic French brasserie at street level, a piano bar above it, and a proper jazz club on top for the weekend bands - South London's closest answer to a Soho jazz supper club, at Kennington prices.
restaurants.opNote: Live music most nights; club shows are ticketed separately from dinner (usually £10-20), so book the table and the show together. Piano bar sets are typically free.

restaurants.name: The Bull's Head
restaurants.style: Riverside gastropub with a dedicated jazz room
restaurants.whyGo: A jazz venue since 1959 - the same year Ronnie Scott's opened - and once nicknamed the suburban Ronnie Scott's: Coleman Hawkins, Ben Webster and Stan Tracey all played the back room, and a young Mick Jagger appeared here too. The music room still runs seven nights a week behind a working Young's gastropub on the Thames towpath.
restaurants.opNote: Music room seats around 70 and is ticketed separately from the pub; the dining rooms and riverside bar are normal pub service. Check the gig listing before travelling - the room is the point.

restaurants.name: The Montpelier
restaurants.whyGo: A Peckham corner local where the Sunday roast comes with a live jazz trio from 7.30pm - the current kitchen residency (Rocco) grills whole fish and shucks some of the better oysters in South London the rest of the week.
restaurants.opNote: Jazz is SUNDAYS ONLY, from 7.30pm - the rest of the week is quiz nights and DJs. The kitchen is a residency and changes hands, so check who is cooking before recommending the food specifically.

restaurants.name: Corner Corner
restaurants.style: Food hall, farm shop and jazz club
restaurants.whyGo: Opened 2025 on the Canada Water regeneration site - a food hall, a working farm shop and a jazz club under one roof, the first real food destination this part of Southwark has had.

restaurants.name: Hawley Wharf
restaurants.whyGo: The newer, purpose-built food courts inside Camden Market on the canal side - distinct from the older stalls, and the covered option when the rest of the market is a crush.
restaurants.opNote: 11:30am-11pm daily. Effectively part of Camden Market, but the food-hall element deserves its own row - it is a different experience from the outdoor stalls.

restaurants.name: Metropolis Vauxhall
restaurants.style: Food hall with the longest bar in south London
restaurants.whyGo: Independent kitchens and what is billed as the longest bar in south London, opened 2024 on Albert Embankment - live entertainment most nights on top of the food.

restaurants.name: Harrods Dining Hall
restaurants.style: Food hall inside a department store
restaurants.whyGo: A live-music dining hall inside Harrods itself - the department-store equivalent of a food hall, and priced accordingly rather than as a casual street-food stop.
restaurants.opNote: Considerably more expensive than the other halls on this list - it is Harrods. Book ahead; walk-ins are not reliable.

restaurants.name: Canteen Food Hall & Bar
restaurants.style: Food hall under a tree-canopy design
restaurants.whyGo: Part of Greenwich Peninsula's Design District, with a distinctive tree-canopy roof - close enough to the O2 to be a sensible stop before or after a show.

restaurants.name: Goods Way
restaurants.style: New Orleans-style food and music hall
restaurants.whyGo: A New Orleans-themed food and live-music hall a few minutes from the station - one of the few King's Cross food halls built around music as much as food.

restaurants.name: Pergola on the Wharf
restaurants.whyGo: A greenhouse-like rooftop food hall on top of Crossrail Place, wrapped in plants - one of the more distinctive rooms among the Wharf's food halls rather than another basement.

restaurants.name: Market Place Food Hall Vauxhall
restaurants.whyGo: Vauxhall's other new food hall alongside Metropolis - a different brand, a different building, and worth distinguishing between the two rather than treating Vauxhall as having just one.

restaurants.name: Hackney Bridge
restaurants.whyGo: A canal-side food and drink hub on the edge of Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, in Hackney Wick's old industrial buildings - kitchens, bars and studio space together.

restaurants.name: The Cheese Barge
restaurants.whyGo: A 96-foot double-decker barge moored on the canal at Paddington Basin, serving British cheese in small plates and a set menu - genuinely eating on the water rather than beside it.
restaurants.opNote: Named in a YouTube travel-guide review of Paddington's hidden spots. Book ahead - a moored barge has fixed, limited covers.

restaurants.name: Short Road Pizza
restaurants.address: William The Fourth, 816 High Road, Leyton
restaurants.whyGo: The most decorated pizza in Britain right now, cooked in the back of a Leyton brewery pub. Romana bases - thin, long-fermented, crisp to the edge - with American toppings on them.
restaurants.opNote: A RESIDENCY, NOT A RESTAURANT. Runs inside Exale Brewery's pubs - William The Fourth in Leyton and Three Colts in Bethnal Green - so the kitchen's hours are shorter than the pub's. Founded by Ugo and Kate on Short Road, Leytonstone.
restaurants.signals: National Pizza of the Year 2025; Time Out world's 3rd best pizza

restaurants.name: Alley Cats Pizza
restaurants.whyGo: The New York-style pizzeria that all three 2026 London lists name - eighteen-inch pies, Southern Italian ingredients, and a room that behaves like a Brooklyn slice joint rather than a trattoria.
restaurants.opNote: Marylebone is the original; a second site sits at 342 King's Road, Chelsea. Despite the New York framing, the restaurants sell whole pies rather than slices - the Portobello Road site is the one adding a slice hatch.
restaurants.signals: Named by Time Out, Country & Town House and The Infatuation

restaurants.name: Yard Sale Pizza
restaurants.whyGo: Started in a back-yard oven in Homerton in 2014 and grew into east London's default good pizza without ever becoming a chain you would avoid. British ingredients, proper vegan options, and consistent across every branch.
restaurants.opNote: Six London sites - Clapton, East Dulwich, Hackney Road, Leytonstone, Walthamstow and Finsbury Park. Clapton is the original.

restaurants.name: Rudy's Pizza Napoletana
restaurants.whyGo: Naples by way of Manchester, and AVPN-accredited - which means the dough, the flour and the oven all meet the Neapolitan association's own standard. The most reliable cheap Neapolitan pizza in central London.
restaurants.opNote: Several London sites including Soho (80 Wardour Street), Shoreditch High Street (Montacute Yards) and Spitalfields (27 Spital Square). Consistent enough that the branch barely matters.
restaurants.signals: AVPN accredited; named by Time Out and Country & Town House

restaurants.name: Ria's
restaurants.address: 29 All Saints Rd, London W11 1HE, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Thick, crisp-edged Detroit pies - baked in a rectangular steel pan so the cheese caramelises against the sides - matched to a natural wine list. Almost nothing else in London commits to this style.
restaurants.opNote: Founded 2023 by a husband-and-wife pair out of tech. Notting Hill is the original; a second site opened in Soho at 29 Foubert's Place, W1F 7QF, with a downstairs wine cave.
restaurants.signals: Named by Time Out and The Infatuation

restaurants.name: Spring Street Pizza
restaurants.whyGo: A Michelin-starred chef leaving fine dining to make eighteen-inch New York slices under a railway arch. The dough is a biga fermented past forty-eight hours, which is where the thin, foldable, properly charred base comes from.
restaurants.opNote: Tom Kemble, previously of Bonhams, opened this in 2025 in the arches off O'Meara Street - a few minutes from Borough Market, London Bridge and the Shard.
restaurants.signals: Named by Time Out and The Infatuation

restaurants.name: Vincenzo's
restaurants.whyGo: Twenty-inch pies cut into slices you eat standing up - the closest thing London has to an actual New York slice shop, rather than a restaurant doing New York pizza.
restaurants.opNote: Slices are grab-and-go from 5pm; whole 16-inch pizzas are takeaway. The original Vincenzo's is in Bushey, outside London - the Shoreditch site opened late 2025.
restaurants.signals: Named by Time Out and The Infatuation

restaurants.name: Napoli on the Road Soho
restaurants.style: Neapolitan, with a pizza tasting menu
restaurants.whyGo: London's first pizza tasting menu, from the pizzaiolo whose Chiswick room has been named Europe's best three years running. Seven courses, four of them pizza, in a basement under the a la carte floor.
restaurants.opNote: TWO FORMATS IN ONE BUILDING. Ground floor is a la carte and seasonal; the basement runs the tasting menu at around GBP 65 a head, with the wine pairing charged on top. Book the basement specifically - it is not the default.
restaurants.signals: Michele Pascarella - Best Pizza Maker in the World, 50 Top Pizza 2023

restaurants.name: Restaurant Gordon Ramsay
restaurants.whyGo: Three Michelin stars held continuously since 2001, which makes it the longest-running three-star restaurant in London. A small Chelsea dining room rather than a grand one - the reputation is entirely the cooking.
restaurants.opNote: Opened 1998, third star in 2001, and it has never lost it. Bookings open well ahead and go; the lunch menu is the cheapest way in. A quiet room rather than a scene.

restaurants.name: Hélène Darroze at The Connaught
restaurants.whyGo: Three stars for cooking rooted in Darroze's native Landes, in south-west France - a regional French kitchen at the very top end, which London has almost none of.
restaurants.opNote: Third star awarded in 2021. Inside The Connaught, so the room is the hotel's rather than a restaurant's own.

restaurants.name: Alain Ducasse at The Dorchester
restaurants.whyGo: Classical French haute cuisine at three stars, including the Table Lumiere - a private table for six ringed by a curtain of fibre optics, and the single most requested seat in Mayfair.
restaurants.opNote: Inside The Dorchester on Park Lane. Ask about the Table Lumiere specifically when booking; it is not offered by default.

restaurants.name: Dinner by Heston Blumenthal
restaurants.whyGo: CLOSING JANUARY 2027. Two Michelin stars for dishes rebuilt from British recipes as far back as the 14th century - the Meat Fruit, a chicken liver parfait disguised as a mandarin, is the one everybody orders.
restaurants.opNote: CONFIRMED CLOSING in January 2027, when the Knightsbridge lease ends. Anyone planning a 2027 trip should not be sent here without checking first. Overlooks Hyde Park from inside the Mandarin Oriental.

restaurants.name: Bertie Blossoms
restaurants.whyGo: Ed Sheeran's pub, opened with his manager Stuart Camp. Small plates, wine and cocktails rather than anything themed - the ownership is the only way you would know.
restaurants.opNote: Refurbished and reopened March 2025. Deliberately low-key: no memorabilia, and no reason to expect a sighting.

restaurants.name: The Grapes
restaurants.whyGo: A narrow Thames-side pub trading for roughly five centuries, part-owned by Sir Ian McKellen. Dickens drank here and put it into Our Mutual Friend as the Six Jolly Fellowship Porters.
restaurants.opNote: Owned in partnership by Ian McKellen, the director Sean Mathias and Evgeny Lebedev. Tiny - the back balcony over the river seats very few and fills early.

restaurants.name: Lore of the Land
restaurants.whyGo: Guy Ritchie's Fitzrovia pub, pouring beer from his own Gritchie Brewing Company - barley grown on his Wiltshire estate - with a more serious dining room upstairs than the bar downstairs suggests.
restaurants.opNote: Two floors: a proper pub at street level, a restaurant above. The beer is the real tie-in rather than the decor.

restaurants.name: The Fox & Pheasant
restaurants.whyGo: An 1846 back-street Chelsea pub bought by James Blunt and his wife Sofia in 2017 and restored rather than reinvented - two small bars, a garden, and pub cooking done properly.
restaurants.opNote: Hidden on a residential street behind the Fulham Road, which is most of the appeal. The Sunday roast is the meal to come for.

restaurants.name: Porte Noire
restaurants.whyGo: Idris Elba's wine bar with co-founder David Farber, at the foot of the Gasholders building by the canal - around 800 wine bins and one of the larger fine wine rooms in London.
restaurants.opNote: Bar, shop and tasting room in one, so you can drink in or take a bottle away. Charcuterie and small sharing plates rather than a full menu.

restaurants.name: The Yurt Café
restaurants.context: The Royal Foundation of St Katharine
restaurants.dietary: Plant-based milks; vegetarian and vegan options
restaurants.whyGo: A working cafe inside an actual Mongolian yurt, in the grounds of a Limehouse charity that has been on the site since 1950. Full English, focaccias and Mission Coffee Works espresso, served under a felt roof.
restaurants.signature: Full English under a felt roof
restaurants.opNote: A SOCIAL ENTERPRISE, not a restaurant group - profits go to the Royal Foundation of St Katharine's community work in Limehouse. Daytime 9:00-17:00; evening service runs 17:00-20:00 Monday to Saturday with themed nights and live music on Thursdays.

restaurants.name: Feng Shang Princess
restaurants.whyGo: A three-tiered Chinese pagoda, painted red and hung with lanterns, moored on the Regent's Canal at Cumberland Basin - hand-built in the 1980s as the first floating restaurant of its kind in London.
restaurants.opNote: Cantonese and Szechuan cooking; the boat is the reason to book rather than the kitchen, and reviews are mixed on the food. About ten minutes' walk from London Zoo's main entrance. Evenings only Monday to Friday; open from noon at weekends.

restaurants.name: The Crosse Keys
restaurants.whyGo: The former headquarters of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, opened 1913 - marble columns, a glass-domed ceiling and a banking hall the length of the room, at Wetherspoon prices.
restaurants.opNote: Opens at 08:00 on weekdays for breakfast. Order at the bar or through the app; there is no table service by default and no music, which is the house style rather than an off day.

restaurants.name: Hamilton Hall
restaurants.style: Wetherspoon in a railway hotel ballroom
restaurants.whyGo: The former ballroom of the Great Eastern Hotel, off the Liverpool Street concourse - gilded plasterwork, chandeliers and cornicing kept intact, which is not what anyone expects from a station pub.
restaurants.opNote: Grade II listed, and reopened after a long refurbishment. On the station concourse, so it is the most useful of these if you are killing time before a train rather than making a trip.

restaurants.name: The Ledger Building
restaurants.style: Wetherspoon in a Georgian dock office
restaurants.whyGo: An 1800 dock building on West India Quay that once held the West India Docks ledgers, with a colonnaded front and a quayside terrace - and by some distance the cheapest place to eat or drink at Canary Wharf.
restaurants.opNote: On West India Quay, a footbridge from the Canary Wharf towers and next to the Museum of London Docklands, which is free - the two make an easy pairing. Order at the bar or by app.

restaurants.name: The Montagu Pyke
restaurants.whyGo: Pyke's Cambridge Circus Cinematograph Theatre, built 1911 as the last of Montagu Pyke's sixteen cinemas - and the cheapest round anywhere near Soho or the West End theatres.
restaurants.opNote: A Wetherspoon since December 1996. Two minutes from Cambridge Circus, which makes it a realistic pre-theatre option at a fraction of Soho prices.

restaurants.name: ICCO
restaurants.whyGo: A twelve-inch pizza from £3.95, made to order and eaten in, two minutes from Goodge Street - which is roughly a third of what anywhere else in central London charges.
restaurants.opNote: Trading since 1999 and calls itself 'the People's Pizzeria'. The £3.95 is the marinara, which has no cheese; toppings push it up but it stays cheap. Counter-style and busy in the evenings - this is a quick meal, not a night out.

restaurants.name: Masters Superfish
restaurants.whyGo: A south London institution five minutes from Waterloo, buying from Billingsgate daily and frying several kinds of fish rather than just cod and haddock. The mushy peas are the ones people write about.
restaurants.signature: Cod and chips with mushy peas
restaurants.opNote: Prawns and bread and butter arrive unasked while you wait, which is the house tradition. Portions are large enough that the small is usually the right order.

restaurants.name: Nautilus
restaurants.whyGo: Fish fried in matzo meal rather than batter - the Jewish north-London tradition that predates the chip shop as most people know it, and a completely different, lighter crust.
restaurants.opNote: Everything comes coated in matzo meal, in matzo and egg, or grilled. A sit-down restaurant as much as a takeaway, seating around 48. Portions are generous even by chippy standards.

restaurants.name: Faulkners
restaurants.whyGo: A proper sit-down chippy on Kingsland Road that has been there since the early 1980s, with a Turkish side to the menu that reflects the street it is on.
restaurants.opNote: A restaurant rather than a counter - table service, and busy at weekends. The Turkish grill dishes sit alongside the fried fish rather than replacing it.

restaurants.name: Michael's Fish Bar
restaurants.whyGo: The chippy east London locals vote for, at prices central London stopped charging a decade ago - flaky batter, thick chips, no seating and no card machine.
restaurants.opNote: CASH ONLY. A takeaway counter, not a restaurant. Voted the area's best by 61% of Leytonstoner readers.

restaurants.name: Mickey's Chippy
restaurants.whyGo: The Stoke Newington chippy that turns up on every north London list, a few doors from one of the better pubs in the area.

restaurants.name: The Golden Chippy
restaurants.style: Greenwich chippy with a big online following
restaurants.whyGo: A Greenwich chip shop that built a large following on review sites rather than in the food press - fresh fish daily, thick hand-cut chips, and a proper sit-down room behind the counter.
restaurants.opNote: Open 11:00-23:00 Monday to Saturday and 12:00-23:00 on Sundays and bank holidays, which is far later than most chippies. Eat in or take away. Halal preparation is available on request. A ten-minute walk from the Cutty Sark and the market.

restaurants.name: Plates
restaurants.whyGo: The first fully vegan restaurant in Britain to win a Michelin star, awarded in 2025. Kirk Haworth cooks a tasting menu that treats vegetables with fine-dining technique rather than as a substitution exercise.
restaurants.opNote: Run by Kirk Haworth with his sister Keeley. One open kitchen, floor-to-ceiling windows, polished concrete. Tables are released in batches and go quickly - this is the hardest vegan booking in the country.
restaurants.signals: Michelin star - the UK's first for a vegan restaurant

restaurants.name: Gauthier Soho
restaurants.whyGo: Alexis Gauthier turned a classical French restaurant entirely vegan in 2021 - the same townhouse dining room, the same technique, no animal products at all. Very few kitchens at this level have made that switch.
restaurants.opNote: Across several floors of a Soho townhouse, which makes it feel like eating in a private house. Tasting menus are the format.

restaurants.name: Mildreds
restaurants.whyGo: Open on Lexington Street since 1988, which makes it the restaurant that made vegetarian food in London normal rather than worthy. Globally drawn menu, and it went fully vegan without losing the crowd.
restaurants.opNote: Sites in Soho, Camden, Covent Garden, King's Cross and Victoria. Soho is the original and the one worth going out of your way for. It does not take bookings at every site - check before travelling.

restaurants.name: The Gate
restaurants.whyGo: Opened in 1989 in a former artists' studio and still the most serious vegetarian cooking in west London - Indo-Iraqi-Jewish influences from the founding brothers rather than a generic meat-free menu.
restaurants.opNote: Hammersmith is the flagship, in a high-ceilinged studio space. Also in Islington (370 St John Street) and Marylebone. Long-standing enough that it predates almost everything else on this list.

restaurants.name: Tofu Vegan
restaurants.whyGo: Chinese cooking done entirely without meat, and the strongest name on every vegan list in London - three of the four independent guides we read put it top. Aubergine in garlic sauce and the mock-meat dishes are what the queues are for.
restaurants.opNote: Books out well ahead on Upper Street; there are further sites including Spitalfields and Marylebone. Not a substitution menu - most dishes are traditionally vegetable-based Chinese cooking rather than meat imitations.

restaurants.name: Diwana Bhel Poori House
restaurants.dietary: Entirely vegetarian, much of it vegan
restaurants.whyGo: Trading on Drummond Street since 1971 and the oldest of the Euston vegetarian Indian restaurants - dosas, bhel poori and an all-you-can-eat lunch thali that is among the cheapest proper meals in central London.
restaurants.opNote: BRING YOUR OWN ALCOHOL - unlicensed, with no corkage. The lunchtime buffet is the value order. Pine benches and no decor to speak of; it has not changed in decades and that is the appeal.

restaurants.name: Temple of Seitan
restaurants.whyGo: A vegan fried chicken shop that behaves exactly like a fried chicken shop - seitan in buttermilk-style batter, burgers, wings and fries, at chicken-shop prices.
restaurants.opNote: Sites across London including Hackney, Camden, Brixton, Hammersmith, Waterloo and Wood Green. Counter service; some sites are takeaway only.

restaurants.name: Club Mexicana
restaurants.address: St Marks Church, Mercato Mayfair, North Audley St
restaurants.whyGo: Tacos, nachos and burritos built on jackfruit and vegan chicken, started as a market stall and now in Kingly Court - the rare vegan restaurant nobody eats at because it is vegan.
restaurants.opNote: Also at Seven Dials Market and on Commercial Street in Spitalfields. Kingly Court is the sit-down one; the market sites are counters.

restaurants.name: Bar Shu
restaurants.whyGo: The restaurant that introduced London to real Sichuan cooking in 2006 - numbing peppercorn, chilli oil and dry-fried beans, at a time when the city thought Chinese food meant Cantonese.
restaurants.opNote: On the corner of Frith Street and Shaftesbury Avenue, on the edge of Chinatown rather than in it. Dishes are marked for heat and the marking is honest.

restaurants.name: Mandarin Kitchen
restaurants.whyGo: The lobster noodles are the reason - a whole lobster over ginger and spring onion noodles, and the dish most London Chinese restaurants are measured against.
restaurants.opNote: Big round tables and lazy susans; built for groups rather than couples. Long-running and deliberately unmodernised.

restaurants.name: Gold Mine
restaurants.whyGo: Roast duck hanging in the window and carved to order - the Queensway institution people cross London for, and cheaper than Chinatown for the same thing.
restaurants.opNote: Queues at peak times and no bookings for small tables. Duck sells out; go early evening rather than late.

restaurants.name: Dragon Castle
restaurants.whyGo: South London's proper dim sum hall - a full-size Cantonese banqueting room at Elephant and Castle, with trolley-era scale and none of the Chinatown mark-up.
restaurants.opNote: Dim sum is served through the day rather than only at lunch, which is unusual. Large enough to take a group without booking far ahead.

restaurants.name: Tattu London
restaurants.whyGo: Contemporary Cantonese served under a cherry blossom canopy on the sixth floor of the Outernet, laid out as four rooms around an inner courtyard.
restaurants.opNote: The Cherry Blossom dessert - a handmade chocolate tree that fogs when water is poured around it - is what most people book for. Sharing menu around 125 pounds a head.
restaurants.signals: 5 domains across three tiers: SquareMeal, Country & Town House, Luxury London, The London Economic, Secret London

restaurants.name: Hainan House
restaurants.whyGo: Hainanese chicken rice cooked properly - poached chicken, rice cooked in the stock, three sauces - which almost nothing else in London attempts as its main event.

restaurants.name: J Sheekey
restaurants.whyGo: Open since 1896 in a warren of small panelled rooms off St Martin's Court, with a central crustacea bar and a fish pie that has outlasted every fashion London dining has been through.

restaurants.name: Scott's
restaurants.whyGo: Trading since 1851, and the grandest seafood dining room in London. Under-sixes are admitted only at weekend and holiday lunch, and from May 2026 it takes assistance dogs only.

restaurants.name: Bentley's Oyster Bar & Grill
restaurants.whyGo: Shucking since 1916 and now Richard Corrigan's. An oyster bar on the ground floor and a grill room above, which amount to two quite different evenings.

restaurants.name: Seabird
restaurants.whyGo: Fourteen floors up on Blackfriars Road from the team behind Brooklyn's Maison Premiere, with an oyster happy hour daily from 3pm to 6pm - the cheapest way into the view.

restaurants.name: Wiltons
restaurants.whyGo: Founded in 1742 as George William Wilton's shellfish stall near the Haymarket, which makes it older than everything else in the guide by more than a century. Saturday is dinner only and Sunday it shuts.
restaurants.opNote: The certificate on its website is a Michelin Guide listing, not a star. Several published guides report it as a star.

restaurants.name: Parsons
restaurants.whyGo: Chalkboard only, and the menu changes every day with what came in. Whole roasted turbot, gurnard, potted shrimp croquettes, Inverawe smoked salmon with Guinness bread.

restaurants.name: The Seafood Bar
restaurants.whyGo: A Dutch import - the family were Volendam fishmongers from 1984 and opened the first Seafood Bar in Amsterdam in 2012. This is their only London site, and the fruits de mer is what the rest of the room is looking at.

restaurants.name: Randall & Aubin
restaurants.whyGo: The marble counters of the old butcher's shop are still in place and there is a disco ball over the dining room. Over twenty years on Brewer Street, and it takes no bookings at all.

restaurants.name: Manzi's
restaurants.dealDetail: Oyster Hour from GBP2 an oyster, 3-7pm Tue-Sat and all day Sunday; lunch two courses GBP16, three GBP20; theatre menu three courses with a drink GBP29.50.
restaurants.whyGo: Oyster Hour runs 3pm to 7pm Tuesday to Saturday and all day Sunday, with Jersey and Poole rocks from GBP2. Lunch is GBP16 for two courses. A 2023 opening from the Wolseley group, not a continuation of the Chinatown original.

restaurants.name: Oystermen Seafood Bar & Kitchen
restaurants.whyGo: A small Henrietta Street room that expanded to make space for a raw bar, which is the seat to want. Work through the oyster list, then the Dorset brown crab with aioli.

restaurants.name: Applebee's
restaurants.whyGo: A family-run Borough Market fixture since 1999 that started as a fishmonger and turned into a restaurant, with the counter still at the front and live-fire cooking behind it.

restaurants.name: Behind
restaurants.whyGo: Andy Beynon's eighteen-seat horseshoe counter took a Michelin star in January 2021 after roughly twenty days of trading - the fastest in British history. A surprise tasting menu built entirely around fish.
restaurants.signals: Michelin star; The Good Food Guide

restaurants.name: Angler
restaurants.whyGo: A rooftop dining room at the South Place Hotel with an all-seafood tasting menu built around British fish and shellfish - the most formal fish cooking in the City.
restaurants.signals: Michelin star; The Good Food Guide

restaurants.name: Faber
restaurants.whyGo: A light-filled corner room from a pair who ran a seafood pub in the East End first, so the supply lines were already in place. Watch the blackboard; the chalkstream trout tartare is the standing recommendation.

restaurants.name: Orasay
restaurants.whyGo: Jackson Boxer's room, focused on fish and seafood and inspired by the Western Isles in its own words - wood-grilled whole John Dory, Isle of Mull diver scallops.

restaurants.name: Sam's Riverside
restaurants.dealDetail: Set menu two courses GBP26.60, three GBP31.50; oyster happy hour GBP2 an oyster; GBP5 corkage every Monday.
restaurants.whyGo: Two courses GBP26.60 and three for GBP31.50 by Hammersmith Bridge, with an oyster happy hour at GBP2 and GBP5 corkage every Monday - the best-value sit-down fish in the guide.

restaurants.name: Rick Stein
restaurants.whyGo: The TV chef's only London site, on the Mortlake towpath, and the Indonesian seafood curry is the order. Walk the Thames path before or after.

restaurants.name: Furness Oyster Bar
restaurants.whyGo: A stall rather than a restaurant, and both sources that name it say the same thing: it is the grab-and-go oyster fix at Borough Market.

restaurants.name: Bibendum Oyster Bar
restaurants.whyGo: Claude Bosi's seafood bistro on the ground floor of Michelin House, where the platters and the caviar list are the point rather than the cooking.

restaurants.name: London Shell Co
restaurants.whyGo: The Paddington barge operation's first permanent restaurant and fishmonger, with a menu dictated by what has been landed and a long wine list.

restaurants.name: The Baring
restaurants.whyGo: Seventeenth in the country in the 2026 Estrella Damm Top 50, and in The Infatuation's description more sit-down restaurant than pub you can drink in.

restaurants.name: The Drapers Arms
restaurants.whyGo: A Barnsbury pub carried by both the extended gastropub ranking and The Infatuation, and the easiest table in Islington on a Sunday.

restaurants.name: The Macbeth
restaurants.whyGo: Time Out's fourth-best Sunday lunch in London, and it calls the thing a rowdy Portuguese luncheon in a revamped Hoxton boozer.

restaurants.name: The George
restaurants.whyGo: A boozy downstairs and a dining room above it, both serving the roast. Not The George Inn in Borough, which is a different pub and a different meal.

restaurants.name: Roe
restaurants.whyGo: Roe by Fallow at Wood Wharf, and the roast here is creator-backed rather than critic-backed - two video reviewers, no masthead.

restaurants.name: Clapton Country Club
restaurants.whyGo: Sunday lunch with live jazz in an old tram shed, which Time Out puts at #28 and calls a classy alternative to the pub version.

restaurants.name: The Clarence Tavern
restaurants.whyGo: A Stoke Newington gastropub that The Infatuation rates equally for a slap-up meal and for a few pints and a nibble, which is rarer than it sounds.

restaurants.name: The Kerfield Arms
restaurants.whyGo: Twenty-fifth in the country in the 2026 Estrella Damm Top 50 - the higher-ranked Camberwell pub, and the less famous one.

restaurants.name: The Hero of Maida
restaurants.whyGo: Twenty-fourth in the country in the 2026 Estrella Damm Top 50, and named by no London roast list at all - a ranked pub the guides have missed.

restaurants.name: Anchor & Hope
restaurants.whyGo: On The Cut by the Young Vic, long-running, and rarely bookable - it holds most of the room back for walk-ins, which is why the queue starts early.

restaurants.name: Brockley's Rock
restaurants.whyGo: The only London shop in the UK top ten for Takeaway of the Year 2026, on Brockley Road since 2011 on the site of a former Chinese takeaway. MSC-certified cod and a homemade tartare sauce.
restaurants.signals: National Fish and Chip Awards 2026 - Takeaway of the Year, UK top 10

restaurants.name: Stones Fish and Chips
restaurants.whyGo: On the 40-shop National Fish and Chip Awards 2026 shortlist and a UK top-three finalist in two further categories. Serving hake alongside cod while cod stocks recover.
restaurants.signals: National Fish and Chip Awards 2026 - Takeaway of the Year shortlist

restaurants.name: Oliver's Fish & Chips
restaurants.whyGo: Fries in pure rapeseed oil with no animal fats or hydrogenated fats, which keeps a standard plate under 500 calories. Fish daily from Billingsgate, Maris Pipers where possible.
restaurants.opNote: The Whetstone branch has closed; Belsize Park is the only site trading. Sunday opening is stated two different ways on its own site and menu - check before travelling.

restaurants.name: Fishcotheque
restaurants.whyGo: On Waterloo Road since 1972, and the counter two separate London chip shop video channels went out of their way to film.
restaurants.opNote: No working website - the domain that looks official has expired. Trading is corroborated by its own social page and dated third-party reviews, not by a live venue site. Confirm before recommending for a special trip.

restaurants.name: Kennedy's
restaurants.whyGo: Pies baked on the premises - steak and Guinness, steak and Stilton - alongside the fryer, from a business that started about 150 years ago as a butcher's known for its sausages.

restaurants.name: Hobson's Fish & Chips
restaurants.whyGo: Double-fried chips and a light batter across three sites - Porchester Road, St Anne's Court in Soho and Villiers Street off the Strand. The family ran Oliver's in Belsize Park before taking on the Bayswater shop.

restaurants.name: Dishoom
restaurants.whyGo: The Irani cafes of old Bombay recreated in careful detail, and the bacon naan roll that made it a breakfast destination as much as a dinner one.
restaurants.opNote: Any party size can book before 6pm; after 6pm bookings are for groups of six or more only. Most tables are held back for walk-ins either way. Seven London branches; the Branches tab has six named.
